title: Easy-to-override defaults with :where()
summary: :where() adds zero specificity, so base styles never win a fight they should lose.
explanation: Base styles written as .prose h2 have the specificity of a class plus an element. Any later component rule with just one class, like .accent, loses to them, which leads to ever-longer selectors and !important.
Wrapped in :where(), the same selector matches the same elements but counts as zero specificity. Now a single class overrides it, as you would expect: the second heading turns orange.
:is() looks the same but takes the specificity of its most specific argument, so it does not help here.
tryThis: Change :where(.prose h2) back to .prose h2: the .accent heading loses its orange.
Replace :where with :is: the same thing happens.
Wrap the paragraph rule in :where() too, then give a paragraph a class to restyle it.

children.text: Base styles for article content, kept at zero specificity.
One class is enough to override the base style.
